reminder: A semistandard Young tableau fills a Young diagram with positive integers that weakly increase along rows and strictly increase down columns.
definition: A semistandard Young tableau is a [Young tableau](c:young-tableau): a filling of the boxes of a [Young diagram](c:young-diagram) with positive [natural numbers](c:natural-number). It also obeys two rules: entries weakly increase along each row from left to right, and entries strictly increase down each column.
examples: For the shape $(2,1)$, the filling with first row $1,1$ and second row $2$ is semistandard.
For the shape $(3,2)$, the filling with first row $1,1,2$ and second row $2,3$ is semistandard.
Non-example: for the shape $(2,1)$, the filling with first row $1,1$ and second row $1$ is not semistandard, because the first column holds $1$ above $1$ and a column must strictly increase.

steps: Take a semistandard Young tableau of shape $\lambda$.
By definition, it fills the boxes of the [Young diagram](c:young-diagram) of $\lambda$ with positive natural numbers.
So it is a [Young tableau](c:young-tableau).
The semistandard case adds two conditions: rows weakly increase and columns strictly increase.
links.why: It shows which conditions turn an arbitrary filling into a semistandard one.

steps: Take a [standard Young tableau](c:standard-young-tableau) $T$ of shape $\lambda$ with entries $1,\dots,n$, each used once.
Its rows strictly increase, so they also weakly increase.
Its columns strictly increase and its entries are positive natural numbers.
So $T$ is a semistandard Young tableau that happens to use each entry once.
links.why: It shows that every standard tableau is semistandard, so results for the semistandard case apply to it.

reminder: Every sequence in a sequentially compact space has a subsequence that converges to a point of the space.
definition: A [topological space](c:topological-space) $X$ is sequentially compact when every [sequence](c:sequence) in $X$ has a [subsequence](c:subsequence) that [converges](c:limit-of-a-sequence) to a point of $X$.
examples: The closed interval $[0,1]$ is sequentially compact, by the Bolzano–Weierstrass theorem.
Every finite space is sequentially compact, because some point repeats infinitely often in any sequence and gives a constant subsequence.
Non-example: $\mathbb R$ is not sequentially compact, because the sequence $1,2,3,\dots$ has no convergent subsequence.

steps: Take a [compact](c:compact-space) [metric space](c:metric-space) $X$ and a sequence $(x_n)$ in $X$.
By compactness, the sequence has a cluster point $x$.
Every ball around $x$ contains $x_n$ for infinitely many $n$, so pick $n_1<n_2<\cdots$ with $d(x_{n_k},x)<1/k$.
This subsequence converges to $x$, so $X$ is sequentially compact.
links.why: It shows why the two kinds of compactness agree for metric spaces.

reminder: A sequence assigns one term to each natural number, so it lists $a_0,a_1,a_2,\dots$ in order.
definition: A sequence in a set $S$ is a [function](c:function) $a:\mathbb N\to S$ from the [natural numbers](c:natural-number), written $(a_n)_{n\ge0}$ with $a_n=a(n)$. A finite sequence is a function from an initial segment $\{0,\dots,m-1\}$ to $S$.
examples: The rule $a_n=1/(n+1)$ gives the sequence of real numbers $1,\tfrac12,\tfrac13,\dots$.
The Fibonacci numbers $0,1,1,2,3,5,\dots$ form a sequence of natural numbers.
Non-example: the set $\{1,2,3\}$ is not a sequence, because a set has no order and ignores repeats, while a sequence keeps both.

steps: Take a sequence $a$ in a set $S$.
By definition, $a$ assigns to each natural number $n$ one element $a_n$ of $S$.
So $a$ is a [function](c:function) from $\mathbb N$ to $S$.
The sequence case adds that the domain is $\mathbb N$ and that the argument is called an index.
links.why: It lets a learner use every fact about functions for sequences.

steps: Order $\mathbb N$ by $\le$, which makes it a directed set.
A net is a function from a directed set to a space.
So a sequence is a [net](c:net) indexed by $\mathbb N$.
The sequence case adds that the index set is the natural numbers.
links.why: It shows that limits of sequences are the countable case of limits of nets.

reminder: The Serre derivative maps a modular form of weight $k$ to a modular form of weight $k+2$.
definition: For a [modular form](c:modular-form) $f$ of weight $k$, the Serre derivative is $\vartheta_kf=Df-\tfrac{k}{12}E_2f$. Here $D=q\,\tfrac{d}{dq}=\tfrac1{2\pi i}\tfrac{d}{d\tau}$ is the [derivative](c:derivative) in the variable $q$ and $E_2$ is the weight $2$ [Eisenstein series](c:eisenstein-series). The correction term cancels the failure of $Df$ to be modular, so $\vartheta_kf$ is a modular form of weight $k+2$.
examples: For $E_4$ of weight $4$: $\vartheta_4E_4=-\tfrac13E_6$.
For $E_6$ of weight $6$: $\vartheta_6E_6=-\tfrac12E_4^2$.
Non-example: the plain derivative $DE_4=\tfrac13(E_2E_4-E_6)$ is not a modular form, because $E_2E_4$ is not modular.

reminder: The shift operator moves each sequence one place to the right and puts $0$ in the first place.
definition: On the [Hilbert space](c:hilbert-space) $\ell^2$ of square-summable [sequences](c:sequence), the forward shift is $S(a_0,a_1,a_2,\dots)=(0,a_0,a_1,\dots)$. It is a linear [isometry](c:isometry) that is not onto, and its [adjoint](c:adjoint-operator) is the backward shift $S^*(a_0,a_1,\dots)=(a_1,a_2,\dots)$. On the [Hardy space](c:hardy-space) $H^2$, the same operator is multiplication by $z$.
examples: On $H^2$ of the unit disc, $S$ sends $f(z)$ to $zf(z)$, so $1$ goes to $z$ and $z$ goes to $z^2$.
Non-example: the backward shift $(a_0,a_1,\dots)\mapsto(a_1,a_2,\dots)$ loses $a_0$, so it is not an isometry and it is not the forward shift.

reminder: The sine of a number $x$ is the height of the point at distance $x$ along the unit circle from $(1,0)$.
definition: The sine function $\sin:\mathbb R\to[-1,1]$ sends a [real number](c:real-number) $x$ to the $y$-coordinate of the point reached from $(1,0)$ by moving a distance $x$ counterclockwise along the unit [circle](c:circle). Equivalently, $\sin x=\sum_{n\ge0}(-1)^nx^{2n+1}/(2n+1)!$ as a [power series](c:power-series).
examples: $\sin0=0$, $\sin(\pi/2)=1$ and $\sin\pi=0$.
$\sin(x+2\pi)=\sin x$, so the sine function is periodic with period $2\pi$.
Non-example: the cosine function is the $x$-coordinate of the same point, so $\cos0=1$ while $\sin0=0$, and the two functions are different.

reminder: Skolemization replaces each existential quantifier with a new function of the universal variables before it and keeps satisfiability.
definition: To skolemize a closed [first-order](c:first-order-logic) [formula](c:formula) in prenex form, remove each [existential quantifier](c:existential-quantifier) $\exists y$ and replace $y$ by $f(x_1,\dots,x_k)$. Here $f$ is a new function symbol and $x_1,\dots,x_k$ are the variables of the [universal quantifiers](c:universal-quantifier) to the left of $\exists y$. The result is a universal formula that is satisfiable exactly when the original formula is.
examples: $\exists x\,P(x)$ becomes $P(c)$ for a new constant symbol $c$.
$\forall x\,\exists y\,R(x,y)$ becomes $\forall x\,R(x,f(x))$ for a new function symbol $f$.
Non-example: replacing $y$ in $\forall x\,\exists y\,(y>x)$ by a constant $c$ gives $\forall x\,(c>x)$, which fails at $x=c$, so the new symbol must depend on $x$.

reminder: A smooth curve is an infinitely differentiable map from an interval into a manifold or into Euclidean space.
definition: A smooth curve in a [smooth manifold](c:smooth-manifold) $M$, for example in $\mathbb R^n$, is a [smooth map](c:smooth-map) $\gamma:I\to M$ from an [interval](c:interval) $I\subseteq\mathbb R$. Smooth means that all derivatives of $\gamma$ exist and are continuous, and the velocity $\gamma'(t)$ may be zero.
examples: $\gamma(t)=(\cos t,\sin t)$ is a smooth curve in $\mathbb R^2$ that runs around the unit circle.
$\gamma(t)=(t^3,t^2)$ is a smooth curve, although its image has a sharp point at the origin, because $\gamma'(0)=0$.
Non-example: $\gamma(t)=(t,|t|)$ is continuous but not smooth, because $|t|$ has no derivative at $t=0$.

steps: Take a smooth curve $\gamma:I\to M$.
The interval $I$ is a $1$-dimensional smooth manifold, possibly with boundary.
So $\gamma$ is a [smooth map](c:smooth-map) between smooth manifolds.
The curve case adds the condition that the source is an interval of the real line.
links.why: It shows that smooth curves obey every rule for smooth maps, such as the chain rule.

reminder: A smooth structure on a topological manifold is a maximal atlas whose charts overlap by smooth transition maps.
definition: A smooth structure on a topological [manifold](c:manifold) $X$ is a maximal [atlas](c:atlas) of charts whose transition maps are smooth. With it, $X$ becomes a [smooth manifold](c:smooth-manifold). Two smooth structures on $X$ are called diffeomorphic when the two smooth manifolds are [diffeomorphic](c:diffeomorph).
examples: The identity chart $x\mapsto x$ on $\mathbb R^n$ generates the standard smooth structure.
The chart $x\mapsto x^3$ on $\mathbb R$ is not compatible with the standard chart, so it gives a different smooth structure, and $x\mapsto x^3$ is a diffeomorphism between the two.
$\mathbb R^4$ carries uncountably many smooth structures that are pairwise not diffeomorphic.
Non-example: the charts $x\mapsto x$ and $x\mapsto x^3$ on $\mathbb R$ together do not form a smooth atlas, because the transition map $t\mapsto t^{1/3}$ is not smooth at $0$.

steps: Take an [exotic smooth structure](c:exotic-smooth-structure) on a topological manifold $X$.
By definition, it is a smooth structure on $X$ that is not diffeomorphic to the standard one.
So it is a maximal smooth atlas on $X$.
The exotic case adds the condition that the resulting smooth manifold is not diffeomorphic to the standard one.
links.why: It shows that a topological manifold can carry several smooth structures, and that exotic ones are the extra cases.

reminder: A spectral gap is an interval of real numbers that contains no point of the spectrum of the operator.
definition: Let $H$ be a [self-adjoint operator](c:self-adjoint-operator) on a [Hilbert space](c:hilbert-space) with [spectrum](c:spectrum-of-an-operator) $\sigma(H)\subset\mathbb R$. A spectral gap of $H$ is an interval $I\subset\mathbb R$ with $I\cap\sigma(H)=\varnothing$. Often one means the gap above an isolated lowest [eigenvalue](c:eigenvalue) $E_0$, of size $\inf(\sigma(H)\setminus\{E_0\})-E_0$.
examples: The harmonic oscillator $H=-\tfrac12\tfrac{d^2}{dx^2}+\tfrac12x^2$ has spectrum $\{\tfrac12,\tfrac32,\tfrac52,\dots\}$, so $(\tfrac12,\tfrac32)$ is a spectral gap.
A real symmetric $2\times2$ matrix with eigenvalues $0$ and $1$ has the spectrum $\{0,1\}$ and the spectral gap $(0,1)$.
Non-example: multiplication by $x$ on $L^2[0,1]$ has spectrum $[0,1]$, so no interval inside $[0,1]$ is a spectral gap.

reminder: A sphere packing is a set of equal balls in Euclidean space whose interiors do not overlap.
definition: A sphere packing in [Euclidean space](c:euclidean-space) $\mathbb R^n$ is a set of closed [balls](c:ball) of one fixed [radius](c:radius) whose interiors are pairwise disjoint. Balls may touch, so their boundary spheres may meet in a point. The density of the packing is the fraction of space that the balls cover.
examples: In $\mathbb R^2$, discs of radius $r$ centered at the points of a square grid with spacing $2r$ form a packing of density $\pi/4$.
In $\mathbb R^3$, the face-centered cubic packing has density $\pi/\sqrt{18}\approx0.74$, which is the largest possible value, as Hales proved.
Non-example: two balls of radius $1$ with centers at distance $1$ share interior points, so they are not a sphere packing.

reminder: No square of a prime number divides a squarefree integer.
definition: A nonzero [integer](c:integer) $n$ is squarefree when no square $p^2$ of a [prime number](c:prime-number) $p$ [divides](c:divisibility) $n$. Equivalently, $|n|$ is a product of distinct primes, where $1$ is the empty product.
examples: $1$, $6=2\cdot3$ and $30=2\cdot3\cdot5$ are squarefree.
Every prime number is squarefree.
Non-example: $12=2^2\cdot3$ is not squarefree, because $4$ divides $12$.

reminder: A vector bundle over a Riemann surface is stable when every proper subbundle has a smaller slope than the bundle.
definition: Let $E$ be a [vector bundle](c:vector-bundle) over a [compact Riemann surface](c:compact-riemann-surface), with [slope](c:slope-of-a-coherent-sheaf) $\mu(E)=\deg E/\operatorname{rk}E$ and [rank](c:rank) $\operatorname{rk}E$. The bundle $E$ is stable when $\mu(F)<\mu(E)$ for every subbundle $F$ with $0<\operatorname{rk}F<\operatorname{rk}E$, and semistable when $\mu(F)\le\mu(E)$ for all such $F$.
examples: Every line bundle is stable, because it has no subbundle of rank strictly between $0$ and $1$.
On $\mathbb P^1$, the bundle $\mathcal O\oplus\mathcal O$ is semistable but not stable, because its subbundle $\mathcal O$ has the same slope $0$.
Non-example: on $\mathbb P^1$, the bundle $\mathcal O(1)\oplus\mathcal O(-1)$ has slope $0$, but its subbundle $\mathcal O(1)$ has slope $1$, so it is not even semistable.

reminder: A standard Young tableau fills a Young diagram with $1$ to $n$, each once, increasing along rows and down columns.
definition: A standard Young tableau of shape $\lambda\vdash n$ is a [Young tableau](c:young-tableau) that fills the boxes of the [Young diagram](c:young-diagram) of $\lambda$ with the [natural numbers](c:natural-number) $1,\dots,n$, each used exactly once. Entries increase from left to right along every row and from top to bottom down every column.
examples: For the shape $(2,1)$ there are two standard tableaux: first row $1,2$ with second row $3$, and first row $1,3$ with second row $2$.
For the shape $(2,2)$ there are two standard tableaux: rows $1,2$ and $3,4$, and rows $1,3$ and $2,4$.
Non-example: for the shape $(2,1)$, the filling with first row $1,1$ and second row $2$ is not standard, because $1$ is used twice.

steps: Take a standard Young tableau $T$ of shape $\lambda$.
Its rows strictly increase, so they also weakly increase.
Its columns strictly increase, and its entries are positive natural numbers.
So $T$ is a [semistandard Young tableau](c:semistandard-young-tableau) that uses each of $1,\dots,n$ exactly once.
links.why: It shows that a standard tableau is a semistandard one with the extra condition that entries are distinct.

reminder: A $*$-algebra is an algebra with a conjugate-linear map $a\mapsto a^*$ that reverses products and squares to the identity.
definition: A $*$-algebra is an [associative algebra](c:associative-algebra) $A$ over the [complex numbers](c:complex-number) $\mathbb C$ with a map $a\mapsto a^*$ such that $(a+b)^*=a^*+b^*$, $(\lambda a)^*=\bar\lambda a^*$, $(ab)^*=b^*a^*$ and $a^{**}=a$. So $*$ is a conjugate-linear anti-[involution](c:involution). More generally, one can replace $\mathbb C$ by a [commutative ring](c:commutative-ring) with an involution.
examples: The [complex numbers](c:complex-number) with $z^*=\bar z$ form a $*$-algebra.
The algebra $M_n(\mathbb C)$ of matrices, with $A^*$ the conjugate transpose, is a $*$-algebra.
Non-example: the identity map $a\mapsto a$ on $M_2(\mathbb C)$ is not a $*$-structure, because $(ab)^*=ab$ differs from $b^*a^*=ba$ for some $a,b$.

steps: Take a [C*-algebra](c:c-star-algebra) $A$, which is a Banach algebra with an involution $*$.
By definition, $*$ is conjugate-linear, reverses products and squares to the identity.
So $A$ with $*$ is a $*$-algebra.
The $C^*$ case adds a complete norm that satisfies $\|a^*a\|=\|a\|^2$.
links.why: It shows that every $C^*$-algebra is a $*$-algebra, and that the norm is the extra structure.

reminder: A $*$-autonomous category is a closed symmetric monoidal category with an object $\bot$ for which double dualization is an isomorphism.
definition: A $*$-autonomous category is a [closed](c:closed-monoidal-category) [symmetric monoidal category](c:symmetric-monoidal-category) $\mathcal C$ with a [dualizing object](c:dualizing-object-in-a-closed-category) $\bot$: for every object $A$, the canonical map $A\to[[A,\bot],\bot]$ is an isomorphism. Then $A\mapsto A^*=[A,\bot]$ is an equivalence $\mathcal C^{\mathrm{op}}\to\mathcal C$.
examples: Finite-dimensional vector spaces with $\otimes$ and $\bot=k$ form a $*$-autonomous category, where $A^*$ is the dual space.
Sets and relations, with the product of sets as tensor product and $\bot$ a one-point set, form a $*$-autonomous category.
Non-example: $\mathbf{Set}$ with the cartesian product is closed monoidal, but no set $\bot$ is dualizing, because $A\to\bot^{(\bot^A)}$ is not bijective for all sets $A$.

steps: Take a [compact closed category](c:compact-closed-category) $\mathcal C$, so every object $A$ has a dual $A^\vee$.
Let $\bot$ be the tensor unit $I$.
Then $[A,I]\cong A^\vee$, and $A\cong A^{\vee\vee}$ holds by compactness.
So $I$ is a dualizing object and $\mathcal C$ is $*$-autonomous.
links.why: It shows that the unit is a dualizing object when every object has a dual.

steps: Take a $*$-autonomous category $\mathcal C$.
By definition, $\mathcal C$ is a closed symmetric monoidal category.
So $\mathcal C$ is a [closed monoidal category](c:closed-monoidal-category).
The $*$-autonomous case adds an object $\bot$ for which $A\to[[A,\bot],\bot]$ is an isomorphism.
links.why: It shows which extra object turns a closed monoidal category into a $*$-autonomous one.

reminder: A set is star-shaped when one point of the set sees every other point along a straight segment inside the set.
definition: A subset $U$ of a real [vector space](c:vector-space), or of an [affine space](c:affine-space), is star-shaped when some point $p\in U$ has the segment $\{p+t(x-p):0\le t\le1\}$ inside $U$ for every $x\in U$. The point $p$ is called a center of $U$.
examples: Every [convex set](c:convex-set) is star-shaped, and each of its points is a center.
A cross made of two open rectangles that cross in $\mathbb R^2$ is star-shaped with the crossing point as a center, but it is not convex.
Non-example: the annulus $\{1<|x|<2\}$ in $\mathbb R^2$ is not star-shaped, because the segment from any point to its opposite point passes through the hole.

steps: Take a [convex set](c:convex-set) $C$ and any point $p\in C$.
By convexity, for every $x\in C$ the segment from $p$ to $x$ lies in $C$.
So $C$ is star-shaped with center $p$.
Star-shaped sets ask this for one center only, not for every choice of center.
links.why: It shows that convex sets are star-shaped, so results for star-shaped sets cover them.

steps: Take a star-shaped set $U$ with center $p$.
Define $H(x,t)=(1-t)x+tp$ for $x\in U$ and $t\in[0,1]$.
This map stays inside $U$ and is continuous, with $H(\cdot,0)=\mathrm{id}$ and $H(\cdot,1)=p$.
So $U$ contracts to $p$ and is a [contractible space](c:contractible-space).
links.why: It explains why the Poincaré lemma holds on star-shaped regions.

reminder: A state on a $*$-algebra is a linear functional $\omega$ with $\omega(a^*a)\ge0$ for all $a$ and $\omega(1)=1$.
definition: A state on a unital [star-algebra](c:star-algebra) $A$ is a [linear functional](c:linear-functional) $\omega:A\to\mathbb C$ with $\omega(a^*a)\ge0$ for all $a\in A$ and $\omega(1)=1$. It models the [expectation value](c:expectation-value) of each [observable](c:observable) $a$, which is the number $\omega(a)$.
examples: On $M_n(\mathbb C)$, $\omega(a)=\operatorname{tr}(\rho a)$ is a state when $\rho\ge0$ and $\operatorname{tr}\rho=1$, that is, when $\rho$ is a [density matrix](c:density-matrix).
On the algebra of continuous functions on a compact space $X$, $\omega(f)=\int f\,d\mu$ is a state for each [probability measure](c:probability-measure) $\mu$.
Non-example: the trace on $M_2(\mathbb C)$ is positive but has $\operatorname{tr}(1)=2$, so it is not normalized and not a state.

steps: Take a state $\omega$ on a $*$-algebra $A$.
By definition, $\omega(a^*a)\ge0$ for all $a$, so $\omega$ is a [positive linear functional](c:positive-linear-functional).
A state adds the normalization $\omega(1)=1$.
links.why: It shows that states are the normalized positive functionals, so facts about positivity apply to them.

reminder: A stochastic differential equation says that a process changes by a drift term plus a noise term driven by Brownian motion.
definition: A stochastic differential equation has the form $dX_t=b(t,X_t)\,dt+\sigma(t,X_t)\,dW_t$, where $W$ is a [Brownian motion](c:brownian-motion). A solution is a [stochastic process](c:stochastic-process) $X$ with $X_t=X_0+\int_0^tb(s,X_s)\,ds+\int_0^t\sigma(s,X_s)\,dW_s$, where the last integral is an [Itô integral](c:ito-integral).
examples: Geometric Brownian motion $dX_t=\mu X_t\,dt+\sigma X_t\,dW_t$ has the solution $X_t=X_0\exp((\mu-\sigma^2/2)t+\sigma W_t)$.
The Ornstein–Uhlenbeck equation $dX_t=-\theta X_t\,dt+\sigma\,dW_t$ is a stochastic differential equation with additive noise.
Non-example: $\tfrac{d}{dt}X_t=-X_t$ with a random start $X_0$ has no $dW_t$ term, so randomness enters only through $X_0$ and it is an ordinary differential equation solved path by path.

steps: Take an [ordinary differential equation](c:ordinary-differential-equation) $\dot x=b(t,x)$.
Set $\sigma=0$ in $dX_t=b(t,X_t)\,dt+\sigma(t,X_t)\,dW_t$.
Then $dX_t=b(t,X_t)\,dt$, which is the same equation.
So every ordinary differential equation is a stochastic differential equation without noise.
links.why: It shows that the stochastic equation adds a noise term to the deterministic one.

reminder: A Stolz angle at a boundary point of the unit disc is an angle-shaped region that ends at the point.
definition: For a point $\zeta$ on the unit circle and a number $M>1$, the Stolz angle is $S_M(\zeta)=\{z\in\mathbb D:|\zeta-z|\le M(1-|z|)\}$, where $\mathbb D$ is the [unit disc](c:unit-disc). It is a region inside the disc, shaped like an angle with its vertex at $\zeta$ and the radius to $\zeta$ as its axis. A path in $\mathbb D$ approaches $\zeta$ nontangentially when it stays in some Stolz angle, as in a [nontangential limit](c:nontangential-limit).
examples: The radius $[0,1)$ to the point $\zeta=1$ lies in every Stolz angle $S_M(1)$, because $|1-r|=1-r\le M(1-r)$.
In the strong form of Abel's theorem, if $\sum a_n$ converges, then $\sum a_nz^n\to\sum a_n$ as $z\to1$ inside any $S_M(1)$.
Non-example: the path $z_t=1-t+i\sqrt t$ tends to $1$ inside $\mathbb D$ but lies in no Stolz angle, because $|1-z_t|\approx\sqrt t$ while $1-|z_t|\approx t/2$.

reminder: A Stone space is a compact Hausdorff space that is totally disconnected.
definition: A Stone space is a [topological space](c:topological-space) that is [compact](c:compact-space), [Hausdorff](c:hausdorff-space) and [totally disconnected](c:totally-disconnected-space), so every connected subset has at most one point. Equivalently, it is compact Hausdorff with a base of clopen sets, and these spaces are exactly the profinite spaces.
examples: Every finite discrete space is a Stone space.
The Cantor set is a Stone space, and so is $\mathbb N\cup\{\infty\}$, the one-point compactification of $\mathbb N$.
Non-example: $[0,1]$ is compact Hausdorff but connected, so it is not totally disconnected.

steps: Take a Stone space $X$.
By definition, $X$ is compact and Hausdorff, so it is a [compact Hausdorff space](c:compact-hausdorff-space).
A Stone space adds that every connected subset of $X$ has at most one point.
links.why: It shows that Stone spaces are the compact Hausdorff spaces with no connected pieces except points.

reminder: A voting rule is strategy-proof when no voter can get a better result by reporting a false preference.
definition: Let $f$ be a [social choice function](c:social-choice-function) that maps each profile $P$ of [preference relations](c:preference-relation) of the voters to an outcome. The rule $f$ is strategy-proof when, for every profile $P$, every voter $i$ and every false report $P_i'$, voter $i$ likes $f(P)$ at least as much as $f(P_i',P_{-i})$ under the true preference $P_i$. Here $P_{-i}$ lists the reports of all other voters.
examples: A dictatorship, where the outcome is the top choice of one fixed voter, is strategy-proof.
Majority rule between two alternatives with an odd number of voters is strategy-proof, because voting for the preferred alternative is always best.
Non-example: plurality rule with three candidates is not strategy-proof, because a voter whose favorite cannot win may gain by voting for a candidate who can.

reminder: A structure is a nonempty set together with an interpretation of every symbol of a signature.
definition: Given a [signature](c:signature-in-logic) $L$, an $L$-structure $\mathcal M$ consists of a nonempty [set](c:set) $M$, the domain, and an interpretation of each symbol of $L$. A constant symbol $c$ becomes an element $c^{\mathcal M}\in M$, an $n$-ary function symbol $f$ becomes a [function](c:function) $f^{\mathcal M}:M^n\to M$, and an $n$-ary relation symbol $R$ becomes a [relation](c:relation) $R^{\mathcal M}\subseteq M^n$.
examples: $(\mathbb Q,<)$ is a structure for the signature with one binary relation symbol $<$.
A group $(G,\cdot,e)$ is a structure for the signature with one binary function symbol and one constant symbol.
Non-example: a map $g:M^2\to M^2$ cannot interpret a binary function symbol, because its values must lie in $M$ and not in $M^2$.

steps: Take a [group](c:group) $(G,\cdot,e)$ with the inverse map $x\mapsto x^{-1}$.
Use the signature with a binary function symbol, a unary function symbol and a constant symbol.
Interpret these symbols by the product, the inverse and the identity element.
Then $G$ is a structure for this signature that also satisfies the group axioms.
links.why: It shows that a group is a structure together with axioms, which is the view of model theory.

steps: Take an [o-minimal structure](c:o-minimal-structure) on a dense linear order $(M,<)$.
It is a structure for a signature that contains the symbol $<$.
So it has a domain $M$ and interpretations of all symbols.
The o-minimal case adds that every definable subset of $M$ is a finite union of points and intervals.
links.why: It shows that o-minimality is a condition on the definable sets of a structure.

reminder: $SU(2)$ is the group of $2\times2$ complex unitary matrices with determinant $1$.
definition: $SU(2)$ is the set of $2\times2$ complex [matrices](c:matrix) $A$ that are [unitary](c:unitary-operator), $A^*A=I$, and have [determinant](c:determinant) $\det A=1$. It is a [Lie group](c:lie-group) under multiplication, and each element has the form $\begin{pmatrix}a&-\bar b\\b&\bar a\end{pmatrix}$ with $|a|^2+|b|^2=1$, so $SU(2)$ is homeomorphic to the [3-sphere](c:3-sphere).
examples: The identity matrix $I$ and $-I$ lie in $SU(2)$.
The diagonal matrix $\operatorname{diag}(e^{i\theta},e^{-i\theta})$ lies in $SU(2)$ for every real $\theta$.
Non-example: $iI$ is unitary, but $\det(iI)=i^2=-1$, so $iI$ is not in $SU(2)$.

steps: Take the [special unitary group](c:special-unitary-group) $SU(n)$ of $n\times n$ unitary matrices with determinant $1$.
Set $n=2$ in this definition.
The group is now the set of $2\times2$ unitary matrices with determinant $1$, which is $SU(2)$.
The case $n=2$ adds a special form: each element is $\begin{pmatrix}a&-\bar b\\b&\bar a\end{pmatrix}$ with $|a|^2+|b|^2=1$.
links.why: It shows that $SU(2)$ is the smallest case of the family $SU(n)$ and has an extra description by unit quaternions.

steps: $SU(2)$ is the set of solutions of the polynomial equations $A^*A=I$ and $\det A=1$ in $M_2(\mathbb C)$.
Multiplication and inverse are polynomial in the entries of $A$, so they are smooth.
A closed subgroup of $GL_2(\mathbb C)$ is a Lie group, by Cartan's closed subgroup theorem.
So $SU(2)$ is a [Lie group](c:lie-group) of dimension $3$.
links.why: It shows why $SU(2)$ has a Lie algebra and an exponential map.

reminder: A subdivision of a simplicial complex cuts its simplices into smaller simplices and keeps the same underlying space.
definition: A [simplicial complex](c:simplicial-complex) $K'$ is a subdivision of a simplicial complex $K$ when the two have the same underlying space and every [simplex](c:simplex) of $K'$ lies inside a simplex of $K$. Then each simplex of $K$ is a union of simplices of $K'$.
examples: Joining the midpoints of the sides of a triangle cuts it into four smaller triangles, which is a subdivision of the triangle.
The barycentric subdivision of $K$ has one vertex for each simplex of $K$ and is a subdivision of $K$.
Non-example: the boundary of a triangle, which has three edges, is not a subdivision of the filled triangle, because the underlying spaces differ.

reminder: A sublinear operator $T$ satisfies $|T(f+g)|\le|Tf|+|Tg|$ and $|T(cf)|=|c|\,|Tf|$ pointwise.
definition: A sublinear [operator](c:operator) $T$ maps a space of [measurable functions](c:measurable-function), for example an [Lp space](c:lp-space), to measurable functions with $|T(f+g)(x)|\le|Tf(x)|+|Tg(x)|$ and $|T(cf)(x)|=|c|\,|Tf(x)|$. These hold for all $f,g$, all scalars $c$ and almost every $x$.
examples: Every [linear map](c:linear-map) $T$ between function spaces is sublinear, because $T(f+g)=Tf+Tg$ and $T(cf)=cTf$.
The Hardy–Littlewood maximal operator $Mf(x)=\sup_{r>0}\frac1{|B(x,r)|}\int_{B(x,r)}|f|$ is sublinear but not linear.
Non-example: $f\mapsto f^2$ is not sublinear, because for $f=g=1$ we get $|T(f+g)|=4$, which is larger than $|Tf|+|Tg|=2$.

steps: Take a [linear map](c:linear-map) $T$ on a space of measurable functions.
Linearity gives $T(f+g)=Tf+Tg$, so $|T(f+g)|\le|Tf|+|Tg|$ by the triangle inequality.
Linearity also gives $T(cf)=cTf$, so $|T(cf)|=|c|\,|Tf|$.
So $T$ is sublinear, and sublinear operators drop the demand for exact additivity.
links.why: It shows that theorems for sublinear operators, such as interpolation, also cover linear operators.

reminder: A submodule of a module is a subset that contains $0$ and is closed under addition and scalar multiplication.
definition: Let $M$ be a [module](c:module) over a [ring](c:ring) $R$. A submodule of $M$ is a [subset](c:subset) $N\subseteq M$ with $0\in N$, $x+y\in N$ and $rx\in N$ for all $x,y\in N$ and $r\in R$. Then $N$ is a module over $R$ and a [subgroup](c:subgroup) of $(M,+)$.
examples: Every ideal of a commutative ring $R$ is a submodule of $R$, when $R$ is a module over itself.
The kernel and the image of a module homomorphism $f:M\to M'$ are submodules of $M$ and $M'$.
Non-example: $\mathbb N\subset\mathbb Z$ is closed under addition, but it is not a $\mathbb Z$-submodule, because $(-1)\cdot1\notin\mathbb N$.

steps: Take a submodule $N$ of $M$.
By definition, $N$ contains $0$ and is closed under addition.
For $x\in N$, the element $-x=(-1)x$ lies in $N$, because $N$ is closed under scalars.
So $N$ is a [subgroup](c:subgroup) of $(M,+)$, and a submodule adds closure under scalars.
links.why: It shows that a submodule is a subgroup with one extra closure property.

steps: Take an [ideal](c:ideal) $I$ of a commutative ring $R$.
View $R$ as a module over itself, with scalar multiplication given by the product of $R$.
The ideal is closed under addition and under multiplication by elements of $R$.
So $I$ is a submodule of $R$.
links.why: It shows that ideals are the submodules of a ring seen as a module over itself.

steps: Take a field $k$ and a [linear subspace](c:linear-subspace) $W$ of a $k$-vector space $V$.
A $k$-vector space is a module over the ring $k$.
The subspace $W$ contains $0$ and is closed under addition and under scalar multiplication by $k$.
So $W$ is a submodule of $V$.
links.why: It shows that submodule results include the subspace results of linear algebra.

reminder: A subnormal series of a group is a chain of subgroups in which each subgroup is normal in the one before it.
definition: A subnormal series of a [group](c:group) $G$ is a chain of [subgroups](c:subgroup) $G=G_0\ge G_1\ge\dots\ge G_n=\{e\}$ in which each $G_{i+1}$ is a [normal subgroup](c:normal-subgroup) of $G_i$. The $G_i$ need not be normal in $G$. The quotient groups $G_i/G_{i+1}$ are the factors of the series.
examples: In $S_4$, the chain $S_4\ge A_4\ge V_4\ge\langle(12)(34)\rangle\ge\{e\}$ is a subnormal series, although $\langle(12)(34)\rangle$ is not normal in $S_4$.
In the abelian group $\mathbb Z$, the chain $\mathbb Z\ge2\mathbb Z\ge4\mathbb Z\ge\{0\}$ is a subnormal series, because every subgroup of an abelian group is normal.
Non-example: $A_4\ge\langle(123)\rangle\ge\{e\}$ is not a subnormal series, because $\langle(123)\rangle$ is not normal in $A_4$.

steps: Take a [composition series](c:composition-series) $G=G_0\ge\dots\ge G_n=\{e\}$ of $G$.
By definition, each $G_{i+1}$ is a normal subgroup of $G_i$.
So the chain is a subnormal series of $G$.
A composition series adds that every factor $G_i/G_{i+1}$ is a simple group.
links.why: It shows that composition series are the subnormal series that cannot be refined.

reminder: A subrepresentation is a subspace of a representation that every group element maps into itself.
definition: Let $\rho:G\to GL(V)$ be a [group representation](c:group-representation). A subrepresentation is a [linear subspace](c:linear-subspace) $W\subseteq V$ with $\rho(g)W\subseteq W$ for all $g\in G$, that is, an [invariant subspace](c:invariant-subspace). Then $\rho$ restricts to a representation of $G$ on $W$.
examples: In the permutation representation of $S_n$ on $\mathbb C^n$, the line spanned by $(1,\dots,1)$ is a subrepresentation.
For every representation $V$, the subspaces $0$ and $V$ are subrepresentations.
Non-example: in the permutation representation of $S_3$ on $\mathbb C^3$, the line spanned by $e_1$ is not a subrepresentation, because the transposition $(12)$ sends $e_1$ to $e_2$.

steps: Take a subrepresentation $W\subseteq V$ and the inclusion map $\iota:W\to V$.
The group acts on $W$ by restriction, so $\iota$ commutes with the action.
So $\iota$ is an injective morphism in the category of representations.
Hence $W$ is a [subobject](c:subobject) of $V$ in that category.
links.why: It shows that subrepresentations are the subobjects of representations.

reminder: The successor of a natural number $n$ is the next number $n+1$.
definition: The successor map $S$ sends a [natural number](c:natural-number) $n$ to the next one, $S(n)=n+1$. In [Peano arithmetic](c:peano-arithmetic), $S$ is injective and $0$ is not a value of $S$. For an [ordinal](c:ordinal) $\alpha$, the successor is $\alpha+1=\alpha\cup\{\alpha\}$.
examples: The ordinal $\omega+1=\omega\cup\{\omega\}$ is the successor of $\omega$.
Non-example: $0$ is not the successor of any natural number, and $\omega$ is not the successor of any ordinal.

reminder: Any linear combination of solutions of a linear homogeneous equation is again a solution.
definition: Take a [linear differential equation](c:linear-differential-equation) $Lu=0$, where $L$ is linear. If $u_1,\dots,u_k$ are solutions, then every [linear combination](c:linear-combination) $c_1u_1+\dots+c_ku_k$ is also a solution. Such a combination is called a superposition of solutions.
examples: For the [wave equation](c:wave-equation) $u_{tt}=u_{xx}$, the functions $\sin(x-t)$ and $\sin(x+t)$ are solutions, so their sum is also a solution.
The functions $e^x$ and $e^{-x}$ solve $y''=y$, so every $c_1e^x+c_2e^{-x}$ solves it.
Non-example: $y=-1/t$ solves the nonlinear equation $y'=y^2$, but $2y$ does not, because $(2y)'=2/t^2$ while $(2y)^2=4/t^2$.

reminder: A tagged partition splits an interval into subintervals and picks one point, called a tag, in each subinterval.
definition: A tagged partition of a [closed interval](c:closed-interval) $[a,b]$ is a finite list of [real numbers](c:real-number) $a=x_0<x_1<\dots<x_n=b$ together with tags $t_1,\dots,t_n$ such that $t_i\in[x_{i-1},x_i]$ for every $i$. It gives the Riemann sum $\sum_if(t_i)(x_i-x_{i-1})$ that defines the [Riemann integral](c:riemann-integral).
examples: On $[0,1]$, the points $0<\tfrac12<1$ with tags $t_1=\tfrac14$ and $t_2=1$ form a tagged partition.
The partition of $[0,1]$ into $n$ equal pieces, with every tag at the left end, is a tagged partition whose Riemann sum is the left sum.
Non-example: on $[0,1]$, the partition $0<\tfrac12<1$ with tag $t_1=0.9$ is not tagged, because $0.9\notin[0,\tfrac12]$.

reminder: A tame Fréchet space is a graded Fréchet space that is a tame direct summand of a sequence space over a Banach space.
definition: A graded [Fréchet space](c:frechet-space) $F$ has seminorms $\|\cdot\|_0\le\|\cdot\|_1\le\cdots$ that define its topology. Let $\Sigma(B)$ be the space of sequences $(b_k)_{k\ge0}$ in a [Banach space](c:banach-space) $B$ with $\|(b_k)\|_n=\sum_ke^{nk}\|b_k\|_B<\infty$ for all $n$. The space $F$ is tame when there are [linear maps](c:linear-map) $L:F\to\Sigma(B)$ and $M:\Sigma(B)\to F$ with $ML=\mathrm{id}$, both tame, which means $\|Lf\|_n\le C_n\|f\|_{n+r}$ for all $n\ge b$ with fixed $r$ and $b$.
examples: The space $C^\infty(M)$ of smooth functions on a compact manifold $M$, graded by the $C^n$ norms, is tame by Hamilton's theory.
A [Banach space](c:banach-space) $B$ with every seminorm equal to its norm is tame, because $b\mapsto(b,0,0,\dots)$ and $(b_k)\mapsto b_0$ are tame maps with $ML=\mathrm{id}$.
Non-example: a Fréchet space with no chosen grading is not tame, because tameness is a property of a graded space.

reminder: The tangent line to a curve at a point is the line that touches the curve there with the same direction.
definition: For a [function](c:function) $f$ that is differentiable at $a$, the tangent line to its graph at $(a,f(a))$ is the line $y=f(a)+f'(a)(x-a)$, where $f'(a)$ is the [derivative](c:derivative). For a [circle](c:circle), the tangent line at a point is the line through that point that is perpendicular to the radius and meets the circle only there.
examples: For $f(x)=x^2$ at $a=1$, the tangent line is $y=1+2(x-1)=2x-1$.
For the unit circle at the point $(1,0)$, the tangent line is $x=1$.
Non-example: the line $y=0$ meets the unit circle in the two points $(\pm1,0)$, so it is a secant line and not a tangent line.

reminder: The tangent space at a point of a manifold is the vector space of velocities of curves through that point.
definition: Let $M$ be a [smooth manifold](c:smooth-manifold) and $p\in M$. The tangent space $T_pM$ is the set of velocity vectors $\gamma'(0)$ of [smooth curves](c:smooth-curve) $\gamma$ with $\gamma(0)=p$, where curves with the same derivative in a chart give the same vector. It is an $n$-dimensional [vector space](c:vector-space) when $M$ has dimension $n$.
examples: For $M=\mathbb R^n$, every tangent space $T_pM$ is $\mathbb R^n$, and the curve $t\mapsto p+tv$ has velocity $v$.
For the sphere $S^2\subset\mathbb R^3$, $T_pS^2$ is the plane through $0$ that is orthogonal to $p$.
Non-example: the set of all curves through $p$ is not the tangent space, because curves with the same velocity at $p$ must count as one vector.

reminder: A tautology is a propositional formula that is true under every assignment of truth values.
definition: A [formula](c:formula) of [propositional logic](c:propositional-logic) is a tautology when it is true for every assignment of [truth values](c:truth-value) to its propositional variables. A truth table with only $T$ in the last column shows this.
examples: $p\lor\lnot p$ is a tautology, called the law of the excluded middle.
$(p\land q)\to p$ is a tautology.
Non-example: $p\lor q$ is false when $p$ and $q$ are both false, so it is not a tautology.

steps: Take a tautology $\varphi$ of propositional logic.
Every interpretation of $\varphi$ is an assignment of truth values to its variables.
The formula $\varphi$ is true under all of them, so $\varphi$ is true in every interpretation.
So $\varphi$ is [valid](c:validity), and a tautology is validity for propositional logic.
links.why: It shows that a tautology is a valid formula in the simplest logic.

reminder: The tensor algebra of a vector space is the free associative algebra on it, built from all its tensor powers.
definition: The tensor algebra of a [vector space](c:vector-space) $V$ is the [direct sum](c:direct-sum) $T(V)=\bigoplus_{n\ge0}V^{\otimes n}$ of all [tensor powers](c:tensor-product), where $V^{\otimes0}$ is the field of scalars. Its product is concatenation: $(v_1\otimes\dots\otimes v_m)(w_1\otimes\dots\otimes w_n)=v_1\otimes\dots\otimes v_m\otimes w_1\otimes\dots\otimes w_n$. Every linear map from $V$ to an [associative algebra](c:associative-algebra) $A$ extends uniquely to an algebra homomorphism $T(V)\to A$.
examples: If $V=\mathbb R$ has one basis vector $x$, then $T(V)\cong\mathbb R[x]$, the polynomial ring.
If $V$ has the basis $x,y$, then $T(V)$ is the algebra of noncommutative polynomials in $x$ and $y$, where $xy\ne yx$.
Non-example: the polynomial ring $\mathbb R[x,y]$ is not $T(\mathbb R^2)$, because $xy=yx$ there, while $x\otimes y\ne y\otimes x$ in $T(\mathbb R^2)$.

reminder: A tensor operator of rank $k$ is a set of $2k+1$ operators that transform under rotations like the basis vectors of spin $k$.
definition: Let $U(R)$ be a unitary [representation](c:group-representation) of the rotation group [SO(3)](c:so-3) on a [Hilbert space](c:hilbert-space). An irreducible tensor operator of rank $k$ is a family of [operators](c:operator) $T^{(k)}_q$ for $q=-k,\dots,k$, such that each rotation $U(R)$ maps the family into combinations of its own members by the matrices of the spin-$k$ [irreducible representation](c:irreducible-representation). With angular momentum operators $J$ and $\hbar=1$, this means $[J_z,T^{(k)}_q]=q\,T^{(k)}_q$ and $[J_\pm,T^{(k)}_q]=\sqrt{k(k+1)-q(q\pm1)}\,T^{(k)}_{q\pm1}$.
examples: A scalar operator, such as a rotation-invariant Hamiltonian $H$, is a tensor operator of rank $0$.
The position operators form a rank $1$ tensor operator with $T^{(1)}_0=z$ and $T^{(1)}_{\pm1}=\mp(x\pm iy)/\sqrt2$.
Non-example: the single operator $x$ alone is not a tensor operator, because a rotation mixes it with $y$ and $z$.

reminder: A Thom spectrum has the Thom spaces of a compatible family of vector bundles as its spaces.
definition: Let $\xi_n\to B_n$ be [vector bundles](c:vector-bundle) of rank $n$ with maps $B_n\to B_{n+1}$ that pull $\xi_{n+1}$ back to $\xi_n\oplus\mathbb R$. The Thom spectrum is the [sequential spectrum](c:sequential-spectrum) whose $n$-th space is the [Thom space](c:thom-space) $\mathrm{Th}(\xi_n)$, with structure maps $\Sigma\mathrm{Th}(\xi_n)=\mathrm{Th}(\xi_n\oplus\mathbb R)\to\mathrm{Th}(\xi_{n+1})$. Its homotopy groups compute the [cobordism](c:cobordism) groups of the structure that the bundles carry.
examples: The spectrum $MO$ uses the universal bundles over $BO(n)$, and $\pi_*MO$ is the ring of unoriented cobordism classes.
The spectrum $MU$ uses the universal complex bundles over $BU(n)$, and $\pi_*MU$ is the complex cobordism ring.
Non-example: the Thom space $\mathrm{Th}(\xi)$ of one bundle is a space and not a spectrum, so it is not a Thom spectrum.

reminder: The time-ordered exponential solves $U'(t)=A(t)U(t)$ with $U(0)=I$ and puts later times to the left.
definition: For a family of [matrices](c:matrix) or operators $A(t)$, the time-ordered exponential $\mathcal T\exp\int_0^tA(s)\,ds$ is the solution $U(t)$ of the [ordinary differential equation](c:ordinary-differential-equation) $U'(t)=A(t)U(t)$ with $U(0)=I$. It equals the Dyson series $\sum_{n\ge0}\int_{t\ge s_1\ge\dots\ge s_n\ge0}A(s_1)\cdots A(s_n)\,ds_1\cdots ds_n$, where later times stand to the left.
examples: If $A(t)=A$ is constant, then $\mathcal T\exp\int_0^tA\,ds=e^{tA}$, the [matrix exponential](c:matrix-exponential).
If the matrices $A(s)$ commute with each other, then $\mathcal T\exp\int_0^tA(s)\,ds=\exp\int_0^tA(s)\,ds$.
Non-example: for noncommuting $A(s)$, the plain exponential $\exp\int_0^tA(s)\,ds$ is in general not the time-ordered exponential, and the Magnus expansion adds the missing commutator terms.

steps: Take a constant matrix $A$ and set $A(s)=A$ for all $s$.
The Dyson term of order $n$ is $A^n$ times the volume $t^n/n!$ of the region $t\ge s_1\ge\dots\ge s_n\ge0$.
Summing over $n$ gives $\sum_nt^nA^n/n!=e^{tA}$.
So the time-ordered exponential reduces to the [matrix exponential](c:matrix-exponential) in the constant case.
links.why: It shows that the time-ordered exponential is the right replacement of $e^{tA}$ when $A$ changes with time.

reminder: The Tjurina algebra of a hypersurface germ is the ring of germs modulo $f$ and all its partial derivatives.
definition: Let $f\in\mathcal O_n=\mathbb C\{x_1,\dots,x_n\}$ be a [holomorphic](c:holomorphic-function) germ that defines a [hypersurface](c:hypersurface) singularity at $0$. Its Tjurina algebra is the [quotient ring](c:quotient-ring) $T_f=\mathcal O_n/(f,\partial f/\partial x_1,\dots,\partial f/\partial x_n)$ by the ideal generated by $f$ and its [partial derivatives](c:partial-derivative). Its dimension is the Tjurina number, and it is finite exactly when the singularity is [isolated](c:isolated-singularity).
examples: For $f=x^2$ in one variable, $T_f=\mathbb C\{x\}/(x^2,2x)=\mathbb C\{x\}/(x)\cong\mathbb C$ has dimension $1$.
For the cusp $f=x^2+y^3$, $T_f=\mathbb C\{x,y\}/(x,y^2)$ has the basis $1,y$ and dimension $2$.

Non-example: the [Milnor algebra](c:milnor-algebra) $\mathcal O_n/(\partial f/\partial x_1,\dots,\partial f/\partial x_n)$ leaves $f$ out of the ideal, so it is not the Tjurina algebra, but the two agree when $f$ is quasi-homogeneous.

reminder: A torsion element of a group has finite order, so one of its positive powers is the identity.
definition:
An element $g$ of a [group](c:group) is a torsion element when it has finite [order](c:order-of-an-element), that is, $g^n=e$ for some integer $n\ge1$; in an additive group the condition is $ng=0$. A group is torsion when all its elements are, and torsion-free when only $e$ is. In differential geometry the word names a different object: the torsion of a [connection](c:connection) $
abla$ is the tensor $T(X,Y)=
abla_XY-
abla_YX-[X,Y]$.
examples: In $\mathbb Z/6$ the element $2$ is torsion, because $3\cdot2=0$.
In the circle group, the roots of unity are torsion elements and $e^{i}$ is not.
The Levi-Civita connection of a Riemannian manifold has torsion $T=0$.
Non-example: $1\in\mathbb Z$ is not torsion, because $n\cdot1=n\ne0$ for every $n\ge1$.

reminder: The torsion subgroup of an abelian group is the subgroup of all its elements of finite order.
definition: The torsion subgroup of an [abelian group](c:abelian-group) $A$ is $\operatorname{tors}(A)=\{a\in A:na=0\text{ for some integer }n\ge1\}$, the set of [torsion](c:torsion) elements. It is a [subgroup](c:subgroup) of $A$, and the quotient $A/\operatorname{tors}(A)$ is torsion-free.
examples: For $A=\mathbb Z/4\oplus\mathbb Z$, the torsion subgroup is $\mathbb Z/4\oplus0$.
The torsion subgroup of $\mathbb Q/\mathbb Z$ is the whole group, and the torsion subgroup of $\mathbb Z$ is $0$.

Non-example: in the infinite dihedral group the elements of finite order are the identity and the reflections, and they do not form a subgroup, because the product of two reflections is a nontrivial translation.

steps: Take $a,b\in\operatorname{tors}(A)$ with $ma=0$ and $nb=0$ for integers $m,n\ge1$.
Then $mn(a+b)=n(ma)+m(nb)=0$, so $a+b$ is torsion.
Also $0$ is torsion, and $m(-a)=-(ma)=0$, so $-a$ is torsion.
So $\operatorname{tors}(A)$ is a [subgroup](c:subgroup) of $A$.
links.why: It shows why the elements of finite order form a subgroup when the group is abelian.

reminder: A tubular neighborhood of a submanifold is an open neighborhood that is diffeomorphic to its normal bundle.
definition: Let $i:X\hookrightarrow Y$ be an [embedding](c:embedding-of-differentiable-manifolds) of [manifolds](c:manifold). A tubular neighborhood of $X$ in $Y$ is an [open neighborhood](c:open-neighbourhood) $U$ of $i(X)$ together with a diffeomorphism from the total space of the [normal bundle](c:normal-bundle) of $X$ onto $U$ that restricts to $i$ on the zero section.
examples: For the circle $S^1\subset\mathbb R^2$, the annulus $\{1-\varepsilon<|x|<1+\varepsilon\}$ is a tubular neighborhood, and the normal bundle is the trivial bundle $S^1\times(-\varepsilon,\varepsilon)$.
A small coordinate ball around a point $p$ is a tubular neighborhood of $\{p\}$, with normal bundle $T_pY\cong\mathbb R^n$.
Non-example: a figure-eight curve in $\mathbb R^2$ is the image of an immersed circle that is not an embedding at the crossing point, so it has no tubular neighborhood.

reminder: In a uniformly convex space, the midpoint of two far apart unit vectors lies well inside the unit ball.
definition: A real [normed space](c:normed-space) $X$ is uniformly convex when for every $\varepsilon>0$ there is $\delta>0$ such that $\|x\|=\|y\|=1$ and $\|x-y\|\ge\varepsilon$ imply $\|\tfrac{x+y}2\|\le1-\delta$. So the midpoint of two unit vectors that are far apart lies strictly inside the unit ball, by a margin that depends only on $\varepsilon$.
examples: Every [Hilbert space](c:hilbert-space) is uniformly convex.
The [Lp spaces](c:lp-space) with $1<p<\infty$ are uniformly convex, by Clarkson's inequalities.
Non-example: $\mathbb R^2$ with the max norm is not uniformly convex, because $x=(1,1)$ and $y=(1,-1)$ have $\|x-y\|=2$ but $\|\tfrac{x+y}2\|=1$.

steps: Take a [Hilbert space](c:hilbert-space) $H$ and unit vectors $x,y$ with $\|x-y\|\ge\varepsilon$.
The parallelogram law gives $\|x+y\|^2+\|x-y\|^2=4$.
So the midpoint satisfies $\|\tfrac{x+y}2\|^2=1-\|x-y\|^2/4\le1-\varepsilon^2/4$.
Take $\delta=1-\sqrt{1-\varepsilon^2/4}$, and then $H$ is uniformly convex.
links.why: It shows that uniform convexity holds in every Hilbert space and has the parallelogram law as its source.

reminder: A code is uniquely decodable when each concatenation of codewords can be read back in only one way.
definition: Let $C$ be a finite set of nonempty [strings](c:string-computer-science), called codewords, over an alphabet. The code $C$ is uniquely decodable when the map that sends a finite sequence of codewords to its concatenation is [injective](c:injective-map).
examples: The code $\{0,10,11\}$ is uniquely decodable, because no codeword begins another codeword.
The code $\{0,01,011\}$ is uniquely decodable although some codewords begin others, because every codeword starts with the symbol $0$ and a $0$ marks the start of each codeword.
Non-example: $\{0,1,01\}$ is not uniquely decodable, because the string $01$ is both the codeword $01$ and the sequence $0,1$.

steps: Take a [prefix code](c:prefix-code) $C$, so no codeword is a prefix of another codeword.
Read a concatenation from the left; exactly one codeword is a prefix of the string, so the first codeword is determined.
Remove that codeword and repeat with the rest of the string.
So the sequence of codewords is determined, and $C$ is uniquely decodable.
links.why: It shows that prefix codes are uniquely decodable, so results for uniquely decodable codes apply to them.

reminder: A formula is valid when it is true in every interpretation, and an argument is valid when true premises force a true conclusion.
definition: A [formula](c:formula) $\varphi$ of a logic with [signature](c:signature-in-logic) $L$ is valid when $\varphi$ is true in every [interpretation](c:interpretation) of $L$, that is, in every structure for $L$ with every assignment of the variables. An argument with premises $\Gamma$ and conclusion $\varphi$ is valid when every interpretation that makes all of $\Gamma$ true also makes $\varphi$ true.
examples: The formula $\forall x\,(P(x)\to P(x))$ is valid.
The argument from $p$ and $p\to q$ to $q$, called modus ponens, is valid.
Non-example: the argument from $p\to q$ and $q$ to $p$ is not valid, because $p$ false and $q$ true make both premises true and the conclusion false.

steps: Take a [tautology](c:tautology), a propositional formula that is true under every assignment of truth values.
Read its assignments as the interpretations of propositional logic.
It is true in every interpretation, so it is valid.
Validity extends this idea to logics with quantifiers, where the interpretations are structures.
links.why: It shows that validity is the general idea and a tautology is its propositional case.

reminder: The wave front set of a distribution records each point and direction where the distribution is not smooth.
definition: Let $u$ be a [distribution](c:distribution) on an open set $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$. A point $(x_0,\xi_0)\in\Omega\times(\mathbb R^n\setminus\{0\})$ is not in $\mathrm{WF}(u)$ when there are a [bump function](c:bump-function) $\varphi$ with $\varphi(x_0)\ne0$ and a [cone](c:cone) $\Gamma$ around $\xi_0$ such that the [Fourier transform](c:fourier-transform-of-distributions) $\widehat{\varphi u}(\xi)$ decays faster than any power of $|\xi|$ as $|\xi|\to\infty$ in $\Gamma$. The wave front set $\mathrm{WF}(u)$ is the set of all other points.
examples: For the Dirac distribution on $\mathbb R$, $\mathrm{WF}(\delta_0)=\{0\}\times(\mathbb R\setminus\{0\})$.
A smooth function has an empty wave front set.
Non-example: $(1,\xi)$ is not in $\mathrm{WF}(\delta_0)$ for any $\xi$, because a bump function supported near $1$ gives $\varphi\delta_0=0$.

reminder: A sequence converges weakly when every continuous linear functional, or for measures every bounded continuous function, gives convergent values.
definition: A sequence $x_n$ in a [normed space](c:normed-space) $X$ converges weakly to $x$ when $f(x_n)\to f(x)$ for every continuous [linear functional](c:linear-functional) $f\in X^*$. For [probability measures](c:probability-measure) $\mu_n$ and $\mu$, weak convergence means $\int\varphi\,d\mu_n\to\int\varphi\,d\mu$ for every bounded continuous function $\varphi$, which is convergence in law for laws of random variables.
examples: In $\ell^2$ the unit vectors $e_n$ converge weakly to $0$, because $\langle e_n,y\rangle=y_n\to0$ for every $y\in\ell^2$.
The point masses $\delta_{1/n}$ converge weakly to $\delta_0$, because $\varphi(1/n)\to\varphi(0)$ for every continuous $\varphi$.
Non-example: the point masses $\delta_n$ on $\mathbb R$ do not converge weakly, because $\int\sin\,d\delta_n=\sin n$ has no limit.

reminder: Probability measures $\mu_n$ converge weakly to $\mu$ when $\int\varphi\,d\mu_n\to\int\varphi\,d\mu$ for every bounded continuous $\varphi$.
definition: Let $(S,d)$ be a [metric space](c:metric-space). A sequence of [probability measures](c:probability-measure) $\mu_n$ on the Borel sets of $S$ converges weakly to $\mu$ when $\int\varphi\,d\mu_n\to\int\varphi\,d\mu$ for every [bounded continuous function](c:bounded-continuous-function) $\varphi:S\to\mathbb R$. By the portmanteau theorem, this is equivalent to $\limsup_n\mu_n(F)\le\mu(F)$ for every closed set $F$.
examples: The point masses $\delta_{1/n}$ converge weakly to $\delta_0$ on $\mathbb R$.
By the central limit theorem, the laws of $(X_1+\dots+X_n)/\sqrt n$ converge weakly to the standard normal law, for independent identically distributed $X_i$ with mean $0$ and variance $1$.
Non-example: the point masses $\delta_n$ on $\mathbb R$ have no weak limit, because the mass escapes to infinity and $\int\sin\,d\delta_n=\sin n$ does not converge.

steps: Take random variables $X_n$ and $X$ with laws $\mu_n$ and $\mu$, which are probability measures on $\mathbb R$.
The statement $X_n\to X$ in [distribution](c:convergence-in-distribution) means $E\varphi(X_n)\to E\varphi(X)$ for bounded continuous $\varphi$.
Since $E\varphi(X_n)=\int\varphi\,d\mu_n$, this says that $\mu_n$ converges weakly to $\mu$.
So convergence in distribution is weak convergence of the laws.
links.why: It shows that convergence in distribution is weak convergence of measures, applied to laws of random variables.
